doc.title: Chico Hamilton interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 30, 2000

title: Writing the book, refusing gossip, and camaraderie of musicians
summary: Publishers want dirt, he refuses; musicians have camaraderie unlike actors.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: Yeah, look forward to that. It’s a long process isn’t it, writing a book?

Oh yeah. Yeah it is. It’s a strange process for the simple reason that the potential publishers want me to write about all the dirty things I know, the bad things I know about people. And I refuse to do this.

You know I’ve noticed there’s a real fraternity amongst musicians, that no one that I’ve talked to has offered those kinds of things. And I’m not really after them but even, like we were talking about Benny Goodman, who apparently was a real difficult person, but the worst anybody’s ever said about him is, “Oh that Benny, what a character.” People don’t want to —

Well people are people. And just because you happened to be blessed so that you can play an instrument and play it well doesn’t mean that if you’re a dirty dude man, if you’re a bad guy, you’re still a bad guy. That does not necessarily mean that you’re going to play bad. You understand?

So people — we do bring our personalities into what we do in our playing. Somewhere down the line it shows up. But I would say overall there’s a camaraderie among musicians as opposed to, for instance you take actors. There’s no camaraderie among actors and it’s for a simple reason. It’s because a musician, in order to make music, we have to play together. Ensemble, right, whatever. An actor, there’s only one part. If you got the part I ain’t working. Out of work.
